ba-w1-q1.question: A subscription video app's main goal is to grow next quarter's subscription revenue. Which of these is a **leading** indicator?
options: Total subscription revenue of the last quarter
Number of free trials started this week
Number of subscribers who cancelled last month
Net profit of the last financial year
ba-w1-q1.explanation: Free trials start today and convert into paid subscriptions a few weeks later, so they signal future revenue in advance: option B is a leading indicator. Trap: option C (last month's cancellations) also looks like 'customer behaviour', but it is an outcome that has already happened, i.e. lagging; options A and D are lagging financial results too.

ba-w1-q2.question: A D2C brand's website had 1,60,000 sessions, 4,000 orders and ₹18,00,000 revenue in a month. What are the conversion rate (orders / sessions) and the AOV?
options: Conversion 4%, AOV ₹450
Conversion 2.5%, AOV ₹11.25
Conversion 40%, AOV ₹4,500
Conversion 2.5%, AOV ₹450
ba-w1-q2.explanation: Conversion = 4,000 / 1,60,000 = 0.025 = 2.5%. AOV = revenue / orders = 18,00,000 / 4,000 = ₹450, so option D is correct. Trap: option B divides revenue by sessions (₹11.25 is revenue per session, not AOV); options A and C misplace a decimal or a zero.

ba-w1-q3.question: One day's data for three stores of a retail chain: Store P: 50 purchases / 1,000 visitors, Store Q: 30 / 200, Store R: 20 / 800. What is the chain's overall visitor-to-purchase conversion?
ba-w1-q3.explanation: Overall = Σ purchases / Σ visitors = (50 + 30 + 20) / (1,000 + 200 + 800) = 100 / 2,000 = 5.0%, i.e. option A. Trap: option B is the simple average of the three store rates (5%, 15%, 2.5%), which gives the small Store Q as much weight as the big stores; options C and D are just one store's rate.

ba-w1-q4.question: A dashboard bar chart shows a customer satisfaction score of 92 for Brand X and 94 for Brand Y, but the y-axis starts at 90. How much longer does Y's bar look than X's, and what is the real difference?
options: About 2.2% longer, both visually and in reality
Visually 2.2% longer, in reality 2 times
Visually 2 times as long, in reality only about 2.2% higher
Visually 4 times as long, in reality 2 points higher
ba-w1-q4.explanation: The axis starts at 90, so the bar heights are 92 − 90 = 2 and 94 − 90 = 4 units: Y's bar looks 2 times as long. The real ratio is 94 / 92 = 1.022, i.e. only about 2.2% higher, so option C. Trap: option D treats 4 as the ratio (4 is just the height of Y's bar); option A would be right only if the axis started at 0.

ba-w1-q5.question: A customer-support team's new KPI is 'tickets closed per agent per day', and a bonus is tied to it. In two months the KPI rose 40%, but complaints rose too. Which guardrail metric best catches this problem?
options: Percentage of tickets reopened within 7 days
Total login hours of each agent
Number of new tickets arriving each day
Average time taken to close a ticket
ba-w1-q5.explanation: Because of the bonus, agents can close tickets without solving them (Goodhart's law). The reopen rate (option A) directly checks whether a closed ticket was really resolved, so it is the right guardrail. Trap: option D (average handle time) also sounds quality-related, but rushing tickets closed makes it look even 'better', so it does not catch the gaming; options B and C measure effort and demand, not quality.

ba-w1-q6.question: An e-commerce site's revenue = sessions × conversion rate × AOV. Next month sessions are expected to fall 4% and AOV will stay the same. By roughly how much (relative %) must the conversion rate rise for revenue to grow 10%?
ba-w1-q6.explanation: The factors multiply: 0.96 × (1 + g) × 1 = 1.10, so 1 + g = 1.10 / 0.96 = 1.1458, i.e. g ≈ 14.6%, option C. Trap: option A adds the percentages (10 + 4 = 14%), which is wrong in a multiplicative tree; option B (10 − 4) also flips the sign, and option D ignores the fall in sessions.

ba-w2-q1.question: A fashion e-tailer's return rate rose from 8% to 10% this quarter. How is this change described correctly?
options: 2 percentage points, which is also a 2% relative increase
An increase of 25 percentage points
An increase of 2 percentage points, i.e. a 25% relative increase
An increase of 10 percentage points, i.e. a 125% relative increase
ba-w2-q1.explanation: Absolute change = 10 − 8 = 2 percentage points; relative change = 2 / 8 = 0.25 = 25%, so option C. Trap: option A treats pp and relative % as the same (2 pp is a 25% relative change, not 2%); option B writes the relative 25% as percentage points by mistake.

ba-w2-q2.question: In a loyalty programme, 300 Gold members spend ₹800 per month on average and 700 Silver members spend ₹400. What is the average monthly spend of all 1,000 members?
ba-w2-q2.explanation: Weighted average = (300 × 800 + 700 × 400) / 1,000 = (2,40,000 + 2,80,000) / 1,000 = ₹520, i.e. option A. Trap: option B is the simple average of the two segment averages, which underweights the larger Silver segment; option C swaps the weights (0.7 × 800 + 0.3 × 400); option D adds the two averages.

ba-w2-q3.question: Lead conversions of two sales reps (fictional data): Asha: warm leads 45 / 60, cold leads 12 / 140. Bilal: warm leads 120 / 180, cold leads 1 / 20. Which statement is correct?
options: Bilal beats Asha in both lead types, so he is ahead overall too
Asha is ahead overall and in both lead types, in all three
Both have equal overall conversion because both have 200 leads
Asha is better in each lead type, but Bilal is ahead overall because 90% of his leads are warm
ba-w2-q3.explanation: Asha: warm 75%, cold 8.6%, overall 57 / 200 = 28.5%. Bilal: warm 66.7%, cold 5%, overall 121 / 200 = 60.5%. Asha leads in every segment, but Bilal got 180 / 200 = 90% warm (easy) leads, so Bilal is ahead overall: option D (Simpson's paradox). Trap: option A looks only at the overall number and assumes Bilal is better everywhere; option C confuses equal lead counts with equal conversion.

ba-w2-q4.question: Orders of a food brand (fictional): last year App 600 orders with AOV ₹500, Web 400 orders with AOV ₹900. This year App 1,500 orders with AOV ₹520, Web 500 orders with AOV ₹950. What is this year's overall AOV, and what happened compared with last year's ₹660?
options: ₹692; both channels' AOV rose, so the overall rose too
₹627.50; both channels' AOV rose, yet the overall fell because the mix shifted towards the cheaper App
₹735; the overall AOV rose
₹660; the overall AOV stayed the same
ba-w2-q4.explanation: This year's overall = (1,500 × 520 + 500 × 950) / 2,000 = (7,80,000 + 4,75,000) / 2,000 = ₹627.50, which is below ₹660. App's share went from 60% to 75%: the mix effect overpowered the rate effect, so option B. Trap: option A uses last year's 60:40 mix (0.6 × 520 + 0.4 × 950 = 692); option C is the simple average of the two AOVs.

ba-w2-q5.question: A SaaS company has 1,000 customers: North has 120 Premium + 280 Basic, South has 80 Premium + 520 Basic. The board asks: 'What % of Premium customers are from the North?'
ba-w2-q5.explanation: The question's denominator is the Premium column total: 120 + 80 = 200. North Premium = 120, so 120 / 200 = 60%, option A. Trap: option B is the row % (120 of North's 400 customers = 30% are Premium), which answers the reverse question; option C is the total % (120 / 1,000); option D is the South's share.

ba-w2-q6.question: Two discount strategies (fictional) were tested in different stores. Strategy P: 30% redemption in urban stores (900 customers), 10% in rural (100 customers). Strategy Q: urban 32% (200 customers), rural 12% (800 customers). After standardising to the combined customer mix (urban 1,100, rural 900), which strategy is better and by how many percentage points?
options: P, by 12 percentage points
Q, by 2 percentage points
They are equal
Q, by 4 percentage points
ba-w2-q6.explanation: Common mix: urban 1,100 / 2,000 = 0.55, rural 0.45. P = 0.55 × 30 + 0.45 × 10 = 21%; Q = 0.55 × 32 + 0.45 × 12 = 23%. Q is better by 2 pp, option B. Trap: option A compares the crude overall rates (P 28%, Q 16%), which are biased by P's urban-heavy mix; option D adds the two segment gaps (2 + 2).

ba-w3-q1.question: A beverage company runs a chi-square test of independence on a contingency table of 4 cities and 3 brands. How many degrees of freedom does the test have?
ba-w3-q1.explanation: df = (r − 1)(c − 1) = (4 − 1)(3 − 1) = 3 × 2 = 6, option A. Trap: option B is the number of cells (4 × 3), and option C is cells − 1, which is the goodness-of-fit formula, not independence; option D adds (4 − 1) + (3 − 1).

ba-w3-q2.question: A survey table of 3 cities × 4 brands has N = 400. Kolkata's row total is 120 and Brand B's column total is 150. Under independence, what is the expected count of the (Kolkata, Brand B) cell?
ba-w3-q2.explanation: E = row total × column total / N = 120 × 150 / 400 = 45, option C. Trap: option A (120 / 4) assumes all four brands are equally popular, which H₀ does not say; H₀ only says Kolkata's brand mix equals the overall mix. Option B (150 / 4) and option D (150 × 150 / 400) use the wrong totals.

ba-w3-q3.question: Of 100 Delhi customers, 60 prefer Brand X and 40 prefer Brand Y; of 100 Mumbai customers, 45 prefer X and 55 prefer Y. Which is the correct result of a chi-square test of independence without continuity correction (α = 0.05; critical values: 3.841 at df = 1, 5.991 at df = 2)?
options: χ² ≈ 2.26, H₀ is not rejected
χ² ≈ 4.51, reject H₀: brand preference and city are associated
χ² ≈ 4.51, H₀ is not rejected because 4.51 < 5.991
χ² ≈ 4.51, and this proves that city causes brand preference
ba-w3-q3.explanation: Column totals X = 105, Y = 95; each row 100, N = 200. E = 52.5 (X) and 47.5 (Y) in both rows. Every cell has |O − E| = 7.5, so χ² = 7.5² × (1/52.5 + 1/47.5) × 2 ≈ 4.51. df = 1, 4.51 > 3.841 ⇒ reject, option B. Trap: option C uses the df = 2 critical value (a 2×2 table has df = 1); option A adds only one row's cells; option D turns association into causation.

ba-w3-q4.question: Below are the observed (O) and expected (E) counts of four cells from a significant chi-square test (3×4 table). Which cell contributes the most to χ²?
options: Mumbai–Brand P: O = 130, E = 115
Delhi–Brand R: O = 48, E = 40
Jaipur–Brand Q: O = 12, E = 20
Lucknow–Brand S: O = 25, E = 15
ba-w3-q4.explanation: Contribution = (O − E)² / E: option A 225 / 115 ≈ 1.96, option B 64 / 40 = 1.6, option C 64 / 20 = 3.2, option D 100 / 15 ≈ 6.67. The largest is option D. Trap: option A has the largest |O − E| = 15, but dividing by a large E makes its contribution small; χ² measures the gap relative to the expected count, not the absolute gap.

ba-w3-q5.question: A 3 × 4 table of 300 customers (3 income bands × 4 brands) gives χ² = 24. What is Cramér's V?
ba-w3-q5.explanation: k = min(3, 4) = 3, so V = √(χ² / (N(k − 1))) = √(24 / (300 × 2)) = √0.04 = 0.20, option C. Trap: option A forgets the square root; option B forgets (k − 1) and takes √(24 / 300); option D uses k = 3 instead of k − 1.

ba-w3-q6.question: Survey 1: Delhi (100) has 55 X / 45 Y, Mumbai (100) has 45 X / 55 Y. In Survey 2 every cell is 4 times larger: Delhi 220 / 180, Mumbai 180 / 220. The 5% critical value at df = 1 is 3.841. Which statement is correct?
options: Survey 1 has χ² = 2.0 (not significant), Survey 2 has χ² = 8.0 (significant), but φ (Cramér's V) is 0.1 in both
Both surveys have χ² = 2.0 because the proportions are the same
In Survey 2, χ² = 8.0 and φ also grew 4 times to 0.4, i.e. a strong association
In Survey 2, χ² = 4.0 (√4 = 2 times), significant
ba-w3-q6.explanation: Survey 1: E = 50 in every cell, χ² = 4 × 5² / 50 = 2.0 < 3.841. Survey 2: E = 200, χ² = 4 × 20² / 200 = 8.0 > 3.841. φ = √(χ² / N) = √(2 / 200) = √(8 / 800) = 0.1 in both, so option A. Trap: option C assumes the effect size grows with N; χ² grew because the evidence grew, while the strength of association is unchanged. Option B forgets that χ² depends on counts.

ba-w4-q1.question: An analyst runs 3 pairwise t-tests, each at α = 0.05, to compare the average bill of 3 store formats. If the tests are treated as independent and there is in fact no difference, what is the probability of at least one false positive?
options: About 14.3%
ba-w4-q1.explanation: FWER = 1 − (1 − 0.05)³ = 1 − 0.857375 ≈ 0.143, i.e. about 14.3%, option D. Trap: option B adds 3 × 0.05; that is only an upper bound (Bonferroni inequality), not the exact probability. Option A assumes each test's 5% stays 5% for the whole analysis.

ba-w4-q2.question: A company compares the sales lift of 4 ad campaigns; each campaign ran in 5 different stores (20 stores in total). What are the degrees of freedom of the one-way ANOVA F-statistic?
ba-w4-q2.explanation: Between-groups df = k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3; within-groups df = N − k = 20 − 4 = 16, so F(3, 16), option B. Trap: option C uses the total df (N − 1 = 19) as the within df; options A and D take the number of groups itself as the df.

ba-w4-q3.question: 4 pricing plans with 10 customers each (N = 40). The ANOVA gives SSB = 120 and SSW = 360. The 5% critical value of F(3, 36) is 2.866. What is the correct conclusion?
options: F ≈ 0.33, H₀ is not rejected
F = 12.0, reject H₀
F = 4.0, reject H₀: at least one plan's mean differs from the others
F = 4.0, reject H₀: all four plans' means differ from each other
ba-w4-q3.explanation: MSB = 120 / 3 = 40, MSW = 360 / 36 = 10, F = 40 / 10 = 4.0 > 2.866, so reject; ANOVA only says that at least one mean differs, so option C. Trap: option D has the same F but stretches the conclusion; which pairs differ is for a post-hoc test. Option B forgets to divide SSB by its df (120 / 10), and option A takes SSB / SSW.

ba-w4-q4.question: A checkout-page A/B test: version A got 120 orders from 2,000 visitors, version B got 150 orders from 2,000 visitors. What is the correct result of a pooled two-proportion z-test (two-sided, α = 0.05, critical value 1.96)?
options: z ≈ 1.89; not significant at the 5% two-sided level
z ≈ 1.89; significant, because the relative lift is 25%
z ≈ 2.67; significant
z ≈ 1.89; significant, because 1.89 > 1.645
ba-w4-q4.explanation: p̂_A = 0.06, p̂_B = 0.075, pooled p̂ = 270 / 4,000 = 0.0675. SE = √(0.0675 × 0.9325 × (1/2,000 + 1/2,000)) ≈ 0.00793. z = 0.015 / 0.00793 ≈ 1.89 < 1.96, so option A. Trap: option D uses the one-sided critical value (1.645) although the test was fixed as two-sided; option C uses only one 1/n in the SE; option B mistakes the size of the lift for significance.

ba-w4-q5.question: An ANOVA of 4 delivery partners gives a significant F. Now all pairwise comparisons are to be done with a Bonferroni correction, family-wise α = 0.05. At what significance level is each pairwise test run?
options: About 0.0083
About 0.0167
ba-w4-q5.explanation: With 4 groups there are m = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6 pairs, so each test is at α / m = 0.05 / 6 ≈ 0.0083, option B. Trap: option A divides by the number of groups (4), not the number of pairs; option D assumes 3 comparisons; option C applies no correction at all.

ba-w4-q6.question: A supermarket chain (fictional) tested 3 shelf layouts in 12 stores (4 stores per layout). Weekly sales (₹ lakh) are shown below. What are the one-way ANOVA F and η², and what is the decision at 5% (F(2, 9) critical = 4.256)?
options: F ≈ 1.72, H₀ not rejected; η² ≈ 0.63
F ≈ 7.75, reject H₀; η² ≈ 1.72
F ≈ 15.5, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.63
F ≈ 7.75, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.63
ba-w4-q6.explanation: Means 11.5, 14.5, 12; grand mean 12.667. SSB = 4 × (1.167² + 1.833² + 0.667²) ≈ 20.67. SSW = 5 + 5 + 2 = 12. MSB = 20.67 / 2 = 10.33, MSW = 12 / 9 = 1.333, F ≈ 7.75 > 4.256 ⇒ reject. η² = 20.67 / 32.67 ≈ 0.63, so option D. Trap: option C forgets to divide SSB by df = 2; option A treats SSB / SSW as F; option B uses that same ratio as η², but η² has SST in the denominator.

ba-w5-q1.question: A stock's market model is R̂ᵢ = 0.2 + 1.3·R_m (both in %). If next month's market return is 2%, what is the stock's expected return?
ba-w5-q1.explanation: R̂ᵢ = 0.2 + 1.3 × 2 = 0.2 + 2.6 = 2.8%, option B. Trap: option A forgets the intercept (only 1.3 × 2); option C adds β instead of multiplying (0.2 + 1.3 + 2); option D forgets to plug in the market return at all (0.2 + 1.3).

ba-w5-q2.question: A model of a bank stock's monthly returns: R̂ = 0.5 + 1.1·Market − 0.4·RateChange, where Market = market return (%) and RateChange = change in the policy rate (percentage points). What is the correct interpretation of −0.4?
options: Holding the market return constant, a 1 percentage point rise in the policy rate is associated with a 0.4 percentage point lower predicted stock return on average
A rise in the policy rate always lowers the stock's return by 0.4%, whatever the market does
The correlation between the stock return and the rate change is −0.4
A 1 percentage point rise in the policy rate makes the stock's return fall by 40%
ba-w5-q2.explanation: A multiple-regression coefficient is a partial effect: with Market held fixed, a 1-unit (1 pp) rise in RateChange changes the predicted return by −0.4 pp on average, so option A. Trap: option C mistakes the coefficient for a correlation (slope and correlation are different things); option B drops both the 'average' and the 'others held constant' conditions; option D misreads the units.

ba-w5-q3.question: A return model with 3 predictors is fitted on 30 months of data and gives R² = 0.64. What is the adjusted R²?
ba-w5-q3.explanation: Adj R² = 1 − (1 − 0.64)(30 − 1) / (30 − 3 − 1) = 1 − 0.36 × 29 / 26 = 1 − 0.4015 ≈ 0.598, option D. Trap: option B uses n − k = 27 in the denominator (forgetting the intercept's df); option C uses n = 30 in the numerator instead of n − 1; option A applies no penalty at all.

ba-w5-q4.question: In a model with 40 observations and 2 predictors, a coefficient has b = 0.85 and SE = 0.30. The two-sided 5% t critical value at df = 37 is 2.026. Which statement is correct?
options: t ≈ 0.35; the coefficient is not significant
t ≈ 2.83; significant (reject H₀: β = 0); 95% CI ≈ (0.24, 1.46)
t ≈ 2.83; not significant, because the 95% CI contains 1
ba-w5-q4.explanation: t = 0.85 / 0.30 ≈ 2.83 > 2.026 ⇒ reject H₀: β = 0. CI = 0.85 ± 2.026 × 0.30 = 0.85 ± 0.608 ≈ (0.24, 1.46), option C. Trap: option D confuses 'the CI contains 1' with 'the CI contains 0'; containing 1 only means β = 1 is not rejected. Option B forgets to multiply by t*, and option A takes SE / b.

ba-w5-q5.question: For a stock's monthly returns: Cov(Rᵢ, R_m) = 18, Var(R_m) = 12, Var(Rᵢ) = 45 (units: %²). What are the market-model β and R²?
ba-w5-q5.explanation: β = Cov / Var(R_m) = 18 / 12 = 1.5. r = 18 / √(12 × 45) = 18 / 23.24 ≈ 0.775, and R² = r² = 324 / 540 = 0.6, so option D. Trap: option B takes r itself as R² (forgot to square); option A divides by the stock's variance (18 / 45); option C inverts the ratio (12 / 18).

ba-w5-q6.question: An auto stock's true model is R = 0.2 + 0.5·Market + 1.5·Sector + ε, where Sector = the auto-sector index return. Regressing Sector on Market gives a slope of 0.4. If an analyst drops Sector and regresses R on Market alone, what will the Market slope be on average?
ba-w5-q6.explanation: Omitted variable bias: simple slope = β_Market + β_Sector × δ = 0.5 + 1.5 × 0.4 = 1.1, option B. The Market slope 'picks up' the sector's effect because the two are correlated. Trap: option A assumes dropping a variable changes nothing; option C adds the two coefficients; option D adds δ directly (0.5 + 0.4) without multiplying by β_Sector.

ba-w6-q1.question: In the residual vs fitted plot of a store-level sales regression, the residuals are centred on zero, but their spread fans out like a funnel as the fitted value increases. What problem does this signal?
options: Multicollinearity
Non-linearity
Heteroscedasticity
Perfect fit
ba-w6-q1.explanation: A spread that grows with the fitted value means non-constant error variance, i.e. heteroscedasticity, option C; it makes the SEs and t-tests unreliable (fix: log y, WLS or robust SEs). Trap: option B shows up as a curve/U-shape, not a funnel; option A is about predictors being correlated with each other, which the shape of the residual plot does not show.

ba-w6-q2.question: In a demand model, regressing 'digital ad spend' on the other predictors gives R² = 0.8. What is the VIF of digital ad spend?
ba-w6-q2.explanation: VIF = 1 / (1 − Rⱼ²) = 1 / (1 − 0.8) = 1 / 0.2 = 5, option D. Trap: option A is the tolerance (1 − Rⱼ²), not the VIF; option B takes 1 / Rⱼ²; option C is just Rⱼ².

ba-w6-q3.question: A simple regression has data for 5 cities, x (population, lakh) = 2, 4, 6, 8, 30. What is the leverage hᵢᵢ of the city with x = 30, and is it high-leverage by the 2p / n rule (p = 2)?
options: h ≈ 0.97; yes, because 0.97 > 0.8
h ≈ 0.77; no, because 0.77 < 0.8
h = 0.2; no, all points have equal leverage
h ≈ 0.97; no, leverage comes only from a large residual in y
ba-w6-q3.explanation: x̄ = 50 / 5 = 10, Sxx = 64 + 36 + 16 + 4 + 400 = 520. h = 1/5 + (30 − 10)² / 520 = 0.2 + 0.769 ≈ 0.97. Threshold 2p / n = 4 / 5 = 0.8, so it is high-leverage: option A. Trap: option B forgets the 1/n term; option C uses only 1/n; option D confuses leverage with the residual, while leverage depends only on x.

ba-w6-q4.question: A sales model has both TV spend and total media spend as predictors (correlation 0.95). The overall F-test is highly significant and R² = 0.85, but both variables' individual t-tests are insignificant. What is the best explanation?
options: Neither variable affects sales; drop them
Multicollinearity: the two carry overlapping information, so their individual SEs are inflated, while together they do explain sales
The F-test is wrong because of heteroscedasticity
The model is overfitted because R² should not exceed 0.85
ba-w6-q4.explanation: When predictors are highly correlated, the model cannot tell which one deserves the effect; the SEs grow (by √VIF) and the individual t-values shrink, while the joint F and R² stay high: option B. Trap: option A reads individual insignificance as 'no effect'; the joint F-test clearly says the two together matter. Option C has no evidence in the question.

ba-w6-q5.question: A predictor has VIF = 9. Compared with the case where it is uncorrelated with the other predictors (VIF = 1), how many times larger is the standard error of its coefficient?
options: 3 times
9 times
81 times
1/9 times (smaller)
ba-w6-q5.explanation: VIF inflates the variance; the SE is the square root of the variance, so the SE is √9 = 3 times larger, option A. Trap: option B applies the VIF directly to the SE (9 is the factor for the variance); option C squares the VIF; option D reverses the direction.

ba-w6-q6.question: The 6 consecutive residuals of a monthly sales regression are: 2, 1, −1, −2, −1, 1. What is the Durbin–Watson statistic and what does it indicate?
options: ≈ 0.92; no problem, because DW lies between 0 and 4
≈ 0.92; negative autocorrelation
≈ 0.92; positive autocorrelation: the residuals come in runs, so the independence assumption is broken
≈ 3.08; negative autocorrelation
ba-w6-q6.explanation: Differences: −1, −2, −1, 1, 2 ⇒ sum of squares = 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 11. Σe² = 4 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 12. DW = 11 / 12 ≈ 0.92, well below 2 ⇒ positive autocorrelation (the residuals come in a positive run, then a negative run): option C. Trap: option A thinks being in the 0–4 range is enough, while the ideal is ~2; option D takes 4 − DW; option B reads the direction backwards.

ba-w7-q1.question: In a salary regression, the 'region' variable has 4 categories (North, South, East, West), and the model has an intercept. How many dummy variables are needed for region?
ba-w7-q1.explanation: k categories need k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 dummies, and the left-out region becomes the reference: option A. Trap: option B (4 dummies) with an intercept creates the dummy variable trap (perfect multicollinearity); option C treats region as a single number coded 1–4, which forces a fake ordering and equal spacing on the regions.

ba-w7-q2.question: In a faculty salary model (₹ lakh), after controlling for experience and rank, the Female dummy (1 = female, 0 = male) has a coefficient of −1.2. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Female faculty earn 1.2% less than male faculty
Among faculty with the same experience and rank, women's predicted salary is ₹1.2 lakh lower than men's on average
Every female faculty member earns exactly ₹1.2 lakh less than a man
The correlation between gender and salary is −1.2
ba-w7-q2.explanation: A dummy coefficient is the average difference from the reference group (male), holding the model's other predictors (experience, rank) constant: option B. Trap: option A misreads the units (y is in ₹ lakh, not logs, so it is not a %); option C drops 'average' and applies an exact gap to every individual; option D mistakes the coefficient for a correlation (a correlation cannot even be below −1).

ba-w7-q3.question: Model: Salary = 12 + 0.6·Exp + 4·Assoc + 9·Full + 2.5·Finance (₹ lakh); reference: Assistant professor, non-Finance field. What is the predicted salary of a Full professor in Finance with 15 years of experience?
options: ₹20.5 lakh
₹36.5 lakh
₹32.5 lakh
₹30.0 lakh
ba-w7-q3.explanation: For a Full professor Full = 1, Assoc = 0, Finance = 1: 12 + 0.6 × 15 + 9 + 2.5 = 12 + 9 + 9 + 2.5 = 32.5, option C. Trap: option B also adds Assoc's 4, as if rank dummies were cumulative; option A forgets the intercept; option D leaves out Finance's 2.5.

ba-w7-q4.question: Interaction model: Salary = 10 + 0.5·Exp + 3·Eng + 0.4·(Exp × Eng) (₹ lakh), where Eng = 1 for engineering faculty. At 10 years of experience, what is the gap in predicted salary between Eng and non-Eng faculty, and what is the Eng experience slope?
options: Gap ₹3 lakh at every experience level; Eng slope 0.5
Gap ₹3.4 lakh; Eng slope 0.4
Gap ₹7 lakh; both groups have slope 0.5
Gap ₹7 lakh; Eng slope 0.9 lakh per year
ba-w7-q4.explanation: Gap = b₂ + b₃·Exp = 3 + 0.4 × 10 = 7; Eng slope = b₁ + b₃ = 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9, option D. Trap: option A treats b₂ = 3 as the gap at every level, but with the interaction 3 is only the gap at Exp = 0; option B adds b₂ + b₃ without multiplying by Exp; option C forgets the interaction's effect on the slope.

ba-w7-q5.question: An analyst puts all three rank dummies, Assistant, Associate and Full, into a model that has an intercept. The software reports a 'singular matrix' error. Why?
options: The sample size is too small
The three dummies sum to 1 in every row, equal to the intercept column: perfect multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap)
There is heteroscedasticity between rank and salary
Dummy variables cannot be used in regression at all
ba-w7-q5.explanation: Every faculty member is in exactly one rank, so Assist + Assoc + Full = 1 = the intercept column. One column is an exact linear combination of the others, so XᵀX is singular: option B. Fix: drop one rank (e.g. Assistant). Trap: option A sounds plausible, but this exact linear dependence stays the same even in a large sample; option C has nothing to do with matrix inversion.

ba-w7-q6.question: Mediation analysis (fictional data): Publications = 2 + 1.5·Exp (path a). Salary = 10 + 0.9·Exp + 0.6·Publications (paths c′ and b). What are experience's indirect effect, total effect and the proportion mediated?
options: Indirect 0.6, total 1.5
Indirect 2.1, total 3.0
Indirect 0.9, total 1.8, with about 50% of the effect running through publications
Indirect 0.9, total 0.9: full mediation
ba-w7-q6.explanation: Indirect = a × b = 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9 lakh per year; total = c′ + a·b = 0.9 + 0.9 = 1.8; mediated share = 0.9 / 1.8 = 50%, option C. The direct effect 0.9 is still non-zero, so this is partial mediation. Trap: option D ignores the direct effect and calls it full mediation; option B adds a and b instead of multiplying; option A takes b alone as the indirect effect.

ba-w8-q1.question: A credit model says an applicant's probability of default is 0.2. What are the odds of default?
ba-w8-q1.explanation: Odds = p / (1 − p) = 0.2 / 0.8 = 0.25, option D. Trap: option A treats the probability itself as the odds; option C inverts the ratio (0.8 / 0.2 = 4, which are the odds of non-default); option B is just 1 − p.

ba-w8-q2.question: In a loan-default logistic model, the dummy 'missed an EMI in the last 6 months' has a coefficient of 0.693. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The probability of default rises by 0.693
The probability of default doubles
Holding other variables constant, the odds of default are multiplied by about 2
The odds of default rise by 69.3%
ba-w8-q2.explanation: Odds ratio = e^0.693 ≈ 2.0, i.e. applicants who missed an EMI have roughly double the odds of default (all else equal), option C. Trap: option B mistakes the odds ratio for a probability ratio; the change in probability depends on the baseline. Option D reads β directly as a % change (without taking e^β); option A reads the coefficient as a change in probability.

ba-w8-q3.question: A churn model: ln(p / (1 − p)) = −3 + 0.04·(monthly data usage in GB). What is the churn probability of a customer who uses 50 GB?
ba-w8-q3.explanation: z = −3 + 0.04 × 50 = −1. p = 1 / (1 + e^1) = 1 / (1 + 2.718) ≈ 0.269, option B. Trap: option A flips the sign (1 / (1 + e^(−1)) = 0.731, the probability for z = +1); option C takes the log-odds as the probability (a probability cannot be negative); option D is e^(−1), which is the odds (0.368), not the probability.

ba-w8-q4.question: On a test of 1,000 transactions, a fraud model has TP = 80, FN = 20, FP = 120, TN = 780. What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 0.40, recall 0.80
Precision 0.80, recall 0.40
Precision 0.86, recall 0.80
Precision 0.40, recall 0.87
ba-w8-q4.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 80 / 200 = 0.40; recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / 100 = 0.80, option A. So the model catches 80% of frauds, but only 40% of the flagged transactions are really fraud. Trap: option B swaps the two formulas; option C takes accuracy (860 / 1,000) as precision; option D takes specificity (780 / 900 ≈ 0.87) as recall.

ba-w8-q5.question: In an NBFC's portfolio only 2% of loans default. A 'model' predicts 'will not default' for every applicant. What is true about this model?
options: Its accuracy is 98%, so it is a good model
Its accuracy is 2% and its recall is 100%
Its accuracy is 98% but its recall is 0: it catches not a single defaulter
Its precision is 98% and its recall is 98%
ba-w8-q5.explanation: All predictions are negative: 98% are right (TN), so accuracy is 98%; but TP = 0, so recall = 0 / (0 + FN) = 0, option C. On imbalanced data accuracy misleads. Trap: option A looks only at accuracy; option B swaps the positive and negative classes; in option D, precision is not even defined when there are no positive predictions.

ba-w8-q6.question: For a lender, approving a loan to a defaulter (FN) costs ₹50,000, and rejecting a good applicant (FP) costs ₹5,000 of lost profit. Above what default-probability threshold should an application be rejected to minimise expected cost?
ba-w8-q6.explanation: Expected cost of rejecting = (1 − p) × 5,000; of approving = p × 50,000. Reject when p × 50,000 > (1 − p) × 5,000, i.e. p > 5,000 / (5,000 + 50,000) ≈ 0.091, option A. Trap: option B is the default 0.5, which treats both costs as equal; option C inverts the ratio (50,000 / 55,000); option D puts only C_FN in the denominator (5,000 / 50,000).

ba-w9-q1.question: An FMCG company shows 40 customers three packaging designs, and each customer rates all three designs on a 1–10 scale. What kind of design is this?
options: A between-subject design with 3 independent groups
A within-subject (repeated-measures) design
A cross-sectional observational survey with no conditions
A matched-pairs design with 2 groups
ba-w9-q1.explanation: Every customer sees all three conditions (designs), so each design's ratings come from the same people: a within-subject (repeated-measures) design, option B. Trap: option A would apply if the 40 customers were split into three groups, each seeing one design; option D applies only to 2 conditions with different but matched people.

ba-w9-q2.question: 10 participants were shown an ad at 4 different frequencies, and recall was measured after each frequency. What are the degrees of freedom of the repeated-measures ANOVA F-statistic?
ba-w9-q2.explanation: Conditions df = k − 1 = 3; error df = (k − 1)(n − 1) = 3 × 9 = 27, so F(3, 27), option C. Trap: option A uses the independent one-way ANOVA df (N − k = 40 − 4 = 36), which leaves the subjects' variation inside the error; option D takes only the subjects' df (n − 1).

ba-w9-q3.question: Purchase intent (1–10) of 6 customers was measured before and after they saw an ad. The (after − before) differences are: 2, 1, 3, 0, 2, 4. What is the result of a paired t-test (two-sided, α = 0.05, critical value 2.571 at df = 5)?
options: t ≈ 3.46; intent rose significantly after the ad
t ≈ 1.41; not significant
t ≈ 8.49; significant
A paired test is wrong; before and after should be tested as two independent samples
ba-w9-q3.explanation: d̄ = 12 / 6 = 2; s_d = √(Σ(d − 2)² / 5) = √(10 / 5) ≈ 1.414; SE = 1.414 / √6 ≈ 0.577; t = 2 / 0.577 ≈ 3.46 > 2.571, option A. Trap: option B takes d̄ / s_d (forgot √n); option C divides by n instead of √n; option D is wrong because two measurements on the same customers are correlated, so the paired test is the right one.

ba-w9-q4.question: 5 participants, 3 ad versions (every participant saw all three). In the RM-ANOVA, SS_conditions = 24, SS_subjects = 60, SS_error = 12. What is the F-statistic?
ba-w9-q4.explanation: MS_conditions = 24 / (3 − 1) = 12; error df = (3 − 1)(5 − 1) = 8, MS_error = 12 / 8 = 1.5; F = 12 / 1.5 = 8.0, option D. Trap: option A also puts the subjects' SS into the error (72 / 12 = 6, F = 12 / 6 = 2), as an independent ANOVA would; option C forgets to divide SS_conditions by its df (24 / 1.5); option B takes SS_conditions / SS_subjects.

ba-w9-q5.question: In an ad-testing study, every participant first watches the 15-second version and then the 30-second version, and the 30-second version consistently gets higher liking. What is the biggest question about this result, and what is the fix?
options: The sample size is small; double the participants
Sphericity is violated; apply the Greenhouse–Geisser correction
The liking scale is ordinal; use a chi-square test
An order / carryover effect: the brand was already familiar by the second ad; counterbalance (half the people watch the 30-second version first)
ba-w9-q5.explanation: Everyone saw the same order, so the 30-second version's advantage may really be 'seeing the brand a second time' (familiarity / carryover): condition and order are confounded. Counterbalancing (half the people in the reverse order) separates them, option D. Trap: option B sounds plausible, but with 2 conditions sphericity holds automatically; option A, a bigger sample does not remove confounding.

ba-w9-q6.question: 4 participants gave recall scores for an ad after 1, 2 and 3 exposures (table below). Critical values: F(2, 6) = 5.143, F(2, 9) = 4.256. Which is the correct repeated-measures ANOVA result?
options: F ≈ 4.11; not significant
F ≈ 27.75; significant
F ≈ 41.6; significant
F ≈ 1.52; not significant
ba-w9-q6.explanation: Grand mean = 70 / 12 ≈ 5.833; condition means 4, 6, 7.5 ⇒ SS_cond = 4 × (1.833² + 0.167² + 1.667²) ≈ 24.67. Subject means 6, 3.67, 7.67, 6 ⇒ SS_subj = 3 × Σ(dev²) ≈ 24.33. SST ≈ 51.67, so SS_error ≈ 2.67, df = 6. F = (24.67 / 2) / (2.67 / 6) ≈ 12.33 / 0.444 ≈ 27.75 > 5.143, option B. Trap: option A treats the data as independent groups (SSW = 27, df 9, F ≈ 4.11 < 4.256); option C divides the correct SS_error by the wrong df = 9; option D takes SS_subjects as the error.

ba-w10-q1.question: An e-commerce company's monthly sales grow about 30% every year, and the festive-season spike also gets bigger each year: +₹2 crore in the first year, +₹3.4 crore in the third year, while the spike always stays about 40% of that year's baseline. Which decomposition model fits better?
options: Additive, because the seasonal spike comes every year
A trend-only model; ignore the seasonality
Multiplicative, because the seasonal swing grows in proportion to the level
Additive, because the trend is linear
ba-w10-q1.explanation: The spike's absolute size grows but stays a constant share (~40%) of the level, i.e. S multiplies the level: a multiplicative model, option C. Trap: option A only notices that 'the pattern repeats'; an additive model would fit if the spike stayed roughly constant in rupees. Option D is also wrong: the trend is 30% compounding (not linear), and the additive/multiplicative choice depends on the size of the seasonal swing.

ba-w10-q2.question: A kirana distributor's weekly sales (₹ thousand): 120, 135, 126, 141. What is next week's forecast using a 3-week trailing moving average?
ba-w10-q2.explanation: Last 3 weeks: (135 + 126 + 141) / 3 = 402 / 3 = 134, option A. Trap: option B is the average of all four weeks (a 4-week MA); option C is the naive forecast (just the last value); option D averages the first three weeks (120, 135, 126), ignoring the latest week.

ba-w10-q3.question: SES with α = 0.3. The forecast for month 1 was F₁ = 100. Actual demand: month 1 = 110, month 2 = 90. What is the forecast for month 3, F₃?
ba-w10-q3.explanation: F₂ = 0.3 × 110 + 0.7 × 100 = 103. F₃ = 0.3 × 90 + 0.7 × 103 = 27 + 72.1 = 99.1, option B. Trap: option C uses the old F₁ = 100 without updating to F₂ (0.3 × 90 + 0.7 × 100 = 97); option A is just F₂; option D swaps the weights (0.7 × 90 + 0.3 × 103).

ba-w10-q4.question: An electronics retailer's Q4 sales are ₹130 crore, and in a multiplicative model the Q4 seasonal index is 1.30. What are the deseasonalised Q4 sales?
options: ₹169 crore
₹128.7 crore
₹130 crore
₹100 crore
ba-w10-q4.explanation: In a multiplicative model, deseasonalised = actual / index = 130 / 1.30 = ₹100 crore, option D: the season's 30% boost is removed. Trap: option A multiplies by the index instead of dividing; option B subtracts 1.30 as if the model were additive (the index is a ratio, not rupees); option C does not adjust for seasonality at all.

ba-w10-q5.question: Quarterly sales: Q1 = 20, Q2 = 30, Q3 = 40, Q4 = 26, and next year's Q1 = 24. What is the 2×4 centred moving average at Q3?
ba-w10-q5.explanation: The first 4-MA (Q1–Q4) = 116 / 4 = 29, which sits between Q2 and Q3; the second 4-MA (Q2–next Q1) = 120 / 4 = 30, which sits between Q3 and Q4. Centred MA at Q3 = (29 + 30) / 2 = 29.5, option A. Trap: options B and C take a single 4-MA, which is not centred exactly on Q3; option D is a 3-point average of Q2, Q3, Q4, which does not smooth out a whole season.

ba-w10-q6.question: Holt's method (Lₜ = αyₜ + (1 − α)(Lₜ₋₁ + Tₜ₋₁), Tₜ = β(Lₜ − Lₜ₋₁) + (1 − β)Tₜ₋₁, Fₜ₊ₕ = Lₜ + h·Tₜ): previous level Lₜ₋₁ = 200, previous trend Tₜ₋₁ = 10, new actual yₜ = 220, α = 0.4, β = 0.5. After updating Lₜ and Tₜ, what is the forecast 3 periods ahead, Fₜ₊₃?
ba-w10-q6.explanation: Lₜ = 0.4 × 220 + 0.6 × (200 + 10) = 88 + 126 = 214. Tₜ = 0.5 × (214 − 200) + 0.5 × 10 = 7 + 5 = 12. Fₜ₊₃ = 214 + 3 × 12 = 250, option D. Trap: option A forgets to update the trend (214 + 3 × 10); option B starts from the actual 220 instead of the level (220 + 36); option C applies only 2 steps (214 + 24).

ba-w11-q1.question: Which of these series is most likely to be roughly stationary?
options: Daily percentage returns of a stock index
The daily closing level of the same index
An app's cumulative total downloads
Monthly revenue of a startup that grows 40% a year
ba-w11-q1.explanation: Daily returns move around a stable mean (about 0) with no lasting trend, so they are roughly stationary: option A. Trap: option B (the index level) behaves like a random walk whose mean and variance change over time; returns are the (percentage) differences of this level. Options C and D have a clear trend.

ba-w11-q2.question: Actual demand over 4 weeks: 50, 60, 40, 50, and the forecasts: 45, 62, 46, 50. What is the MAE?
ba-w11-q2.explanation: Errors (actual − forecast): 5, −2, −6, 0. Mean of |e| = (5 + 2 + 6 + 0) / 4 = 13 / 4 = 3.25, option D. Trap: option A is the mean of the signed errors (bias), where positive and negative misses cancel; option B is the RMSE (√(65 / 4)); option C is the total absolute error instead of the average.

ba-w11-q3.question: Actual sales of 4 SKUs: 200, 250, 100, 50, and the forecasts: 170, 250, 110, 60. What is the MAPE?
ba-w11-q3.explanation: Percentage errors: 30 / 200 = 15%, 0 / 250 = 0%, 10 / 100 = 10%, 10 / 50 = 20%. MAPE = (15 + 0 + 10 + 20) / 4 = 11.25%, option C. Trap: option A is total absolute error / total actual (50 / 600), which is WAPE, not MAPE; option B writes the MAE (12.5 units) as a %; option D is the sum instead of the average. Note: the small 50-unit SKU's 20% error weighs most on the MAPE.

ba-w11-q4.question: A short series: 2, 4, 6, 8, 6, 4. Using the standard ACF formula (5 lag-1 pairs in the numerator, the whole series' Σ(yₜ − ȳ)² in the denominator), what is the lag-1 autocorrelation r₁?
ba-w11-q4.explanation: ȳ = 30 / 6 = 5; deviations −3, −1, 1, 3, 1, −1. Denominator = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 + 1 + 1 = 22. Numerator = (−3)(−1) + (−1)(1) + (1)(3) + (3)(1) + (1)(−1) = 3 − 1 + 3 + 3 − 1 = 7. r₁ = 7 / 22 ≈ 0.318, option B. Trap: option A is an ordinary Pearson correlation on the (yₜ, yₜ₊₁) pairs with separate means, which is not the ACF formula; option C divides the numerator by 5 and the denominator by 6 and takes the ratio of these 'averages'.

ba-w11-q5.question: On a 4-month holdout, actual demand: 100, 120, 80, 100. Model A forecasts: 110, 110, 90, 90. Model B forecasts: 100, 120, 80, 130. One big miss (stock-out or dead stock) is very costly, while small misses are cheap. Which model should be chosen?
options: Model B, because its MAE (7.5) is lower than Model A's MAE (10)
Model B, because 3 of its 4 forecasts are exactly right
Model A: B wins on MAE (7.5 vs 10), but A wins on RMSE (10 vs 15), and big misses are costly
They are equal, because both have an RMSE of 10
ba-w11-q5.explanation: A's errors: −10, 10, −10, 10 ⇒ MAE = 10, RMSE = 10. B's errors: 0, 0, 0, −30 ⇒ MAE = 7.5, RMSE = √(900 / 4) = 15. RMSE squares the errors and penalises big misses more, and here the big miss is what is costly, so option C. Trap: option A looks only at MAE, which treats one 30-unit miss like three small ones; option D computes B's RMSE wrongly.

ba-w11-q6.question: An AR(1) model: yₜ = 20 + 0.6·yₜ₋₁ + εₜ. Today's value is yₜ = 70. What is the forecast 3 periods ahead, ŷₜ₊₃?
ba-w11-q6.explanation: μ = 20 / (1 − 0.6) = 50. ŷₜ₊₃ = μ + φ³(yₜ − μ) = 50 + 0.216 × 20 = 54.32, option B. Step by step too: 62 → 57.2 → 54.32. Trap: option A is only the 1-step forecast; option C jumps straight to the long-run mean (which is the limit as h → ∞); option D takes 0.6³ × 70 and forgets the constant c.

ba-w12-q1.question: A beverage company wants to know whether the favourite flavour (Mango / Lemon / Cola) of 600 respondents depends on their age group (18–25, 26–40, 41+). Which analysis is right?
options: One-way ANOVA
Logistic regression with a numeric outcome
Paired t-test
Chi-square test of independence
ba-w12-q1.explanation: Both the outcome (flavour) and the group (age band) are categorical, and the question is about association: a chi-square test of independence on a 3 × 3 contingency table, option D. Trap: option A would apply if the outcome were numeric (like a rating or spend); option C is for two measurements on the same people.

ba-w12-q2.question: An NBFC wants to predict whether new applicants will default within 12 months (yes / no) based on income, existing EMIs and credit history, and it needs a default probability for each applicant. Which method fits best?
options: Simple linear regression
Logistic regression
Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
Simple exponential smoothing
ba-w12-q2.explanation: The outcome is binary and a probability is needed for each applicant, with several numeric predictors: logistic regression, option B. Trap: option A, a linear model can predict outside 0–1 and is not built for a binary outcome; option D is for time-series forecasting, not for classifying individuals.

ba-w12-q3.question: A retail chain introduced a new store layout in 30 of its stores and recorded each store's monthly sales before and after the layout. What is the best approach to test the layout's effect?
options: A paired t-test on each store's (after − before) difference, ideally with a control group of stores whose layout did not change
A Welch two-sample t-test treating before and after as 30 + 30 independent stores
A chi-square test of independence
A one-way ANOVA treating before and after as two groups
ba-w12-q3.explanation: The same 30 stores were measured twice, so take each store's difference and run a paired t-test; this removes store-to-store variation, option A. Control stores are needed because season or market trends can also create a before/after difference. Trap: option B and option D treat the observations as independent (both ignore the store-level pairing), so they lose power; option C is for categorical data.

ba-w12-q4.question: A new checkout flow costs ₹3,00,000 per month. The site gets 8,00,000 visitors / month and the margin per order is ₹125. The A/B test showed a conversion lift of 0.5 percentage points. What is the break-even lift, and is a rollout profitable at the point estimate?
options: 3.0 pp; no, because 0.5 pp < 3.0 pp
0.03 pp; yes, because the lift is far above break-even
0.30 pp; yes, because 0.5 pp > 0.30 pp (monthly gain ₹5,00,000 vs cost ₹3,00,000)
0.50 pp; break-even equals the observed lift
ba-w12-q4.explanation: Break-even = cost / (visitors × margin) = 3,00,000 / (8,00,000 × 125) = 0.003 = 0.30 pp. At 0.5 pp, extra orders = 8,00,000 × 0.005 = 4,000 ⇒ gain = 4,000 × 125 = ₹5,00,000 > ₹3,00,000, option C. Trap: options A and B misplace the decimal when turning the fraction into percentage points (0.003 = 0.3 pp, neither 3 pp nor 0.03 pp); option D treats the observed lift itself as the break-even.

ba-w12-q5.question: A lending startup's credit model does not use gender or religion, but 'pincode' is a strong predictor. An audit shows that applicants from certain areas have a much lower approval rate, while their actual repayment matches other areas. What is the best response?
options: Nothing needs doing, since the model contains no sensitive attributes
Pincode may be a source of proxy discrimination: check approval and error rates by group, justify the need for pincode or drop / replace it, and keep human review
Keep pincode but set the model's threshold to 0.5 for everyone
Stop taking applications from those areas because the model sees them as risky
ba-w12-q5.explanation: Removing sensitive attributes does not guarantee fairness; pincode can act as a proxy for income, community or religion. When actual repayment is the same but approvals are lower, the model is making more false positives (rejecting good applicants) for those groups: option B's audit-and-fix approach is right. Trap: option A is the false comfort of 'fairness through unawareness'; option C, changing the threshold does not remove the proxy's bias.

ba-w12-q6.question: The marketing team tested a campaign's effect separately in 20 customer segments, each test at α = 0.05. Two segments came out significant, with p = 0.012 and p = 0.0018. If the campaign truly had no effect anywhere, how many false positives are expected, what is the Bonferroni threshold, and which results survive?
options: 1 false positive expected; threshold 0.0025; only the p = 0.0018 result survives
0.05 false positive expected; threshold 0.05; both survive
1 false positive expected; threshold 0.0025; both survive
1 false positive expected; threshold 0.0025; neither survives
ba-w12-q6.explanation: Expected false positives = m × α = 20 × 0.05 = 1. Bonferroni threshold = 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025. 0.0018 < 0.0025 survives, 0.012 > 0.0025 does not, so option A. Trap: option B applies no correction and treats 20 tests like one; option C states the right threshold but forgets to compare 0.012 against it; option D wrongly rejects 0.0018 as well.

ba-w1-q7.question: A fitness app's leadership wants to put one number at the top of the dashboard. Which of these is a **vanity metric** that says the least about engagement?
options: 30-day retention rate of new users
Share of weekly active users among all users
Total app downloads since launch
Repeat workout booking rate of members
ba-w1-q7.explanation: Total downloads till date (option C) only ever goes up, even if people never open the app, so it is a vanity metric. Trap: option B also sounds like a "users" number, but it is the share of active users, which can fall and does show engagement; options A and D measure retention and repeat behaviour, which are real decision KPIs.

ba-w1-q8.question: Of these four numbers on a B2B software company's dashboard, which is a **lagging** indicator?
options: Demo requests received this week
Annual revenue churned last quarter
Value of open deals in the sales pipeline
Free trials started this month
ba-w1-q8.explanation: Last quarter's churned revenue (option B) is a result that has already happened, so it is lagging. Trap: option C (pipeline value) is also in rupees and looks financial, but it signals future deals, so it is leading; options A and D also tell you about revenue before it arrives.

ba-w1-q9.question: Two teams in the same company report 'active users' in the monthly review: the Product team says 52,000 and the Finance team says 38,000. Both use the same data source. What is the most likely reason for the mismatch?
options: A different definition of 'active' (login vs purchase)
One team's database server is very slow
The Finance team rounded off the big numbers
The two dashboards use different chart types
ba-w1-q9.explanation: A gap this large (52,000 vs 38,000) from the same source comes from a different metric definition: which event counts as "active" and how long the time window is. So option A is correct; a KPI needs its full definition written down (numerator, denominator, time window, grain). Trap: rounding (option C) only creates small gaps, not thousands; options B and D are about presentation or speed and do not change the number.

ba-w1-q10.question: A bakery chain's daily sales (units) over five days were 500, 480, 450, 420, 400. The dashboard shows them as a **cumulative** line chart. What will the chart show, and what is the real trend?
options: The line falls from 500 to 400; the real trend is also a 20% fall
The line stays flat at 2,250; sales are stable
The line climbs from 500 to 2,250; real sales grew 125%
The line climbs from 500 to 2,250, while daily sales fell 20%
ba-w1-q10.explanation: Cumulative values are 500, 980, 1,430, 1,850, 2,250, so the line keeps going up. Real daily sales went from 500 to 400, i.e. 400 / 500 − 1 = −20%, so option D. Trap: option C reads the rising line as growth (2,250 is a running total, not growth); option A describes a daily chart, not a cumulative one.

ba-w1-q11.question: An online store's plan for next month has sessions +10%, conversion rate +5% (relative) and AOV −8%. Revenue = sessions × conversion × AOV. What is the expected change in revenue?
ba-w1-q11.explanation: The tree is multiplicative: 1.10 × 1.05 × 0.92 = 1.0626, so revenue rises by about 6.3% (option B). Trap: option A adds the percentages (10 + 5 − 8 = 7%), which is wrong for a product tree; option C forgets conversion (1.10 × 0.92 = 1.012), and option D treats the AOV fall as a plus.

ba-w1-q12.question: Data for Tulsi Bazaar (fictional). Month 1: 5,00,000 sessions, conversion 2.4%, AOV ₹600. Month 2: 4,50,000 sessions, 12,150 orders, revenue ₹70,47,000. What is the % change in revenue, and which driver moved the most (in relative terms)?
options: Revenue −2.1%; conversion +12.5% is the biggest move
Revenue −2.1%; sessions −10% is the biggest move
Revenue −0.8%; conversion +12.5% is the biggest move
Revenue +2.1%; AOV −3.3% is the biggest move
ba-w1-q12.explanation: Month 1: orders = 5,00,000 × 0.024 = 12,000, revenue = 12,000 × 600 = ₹72,00,000. Month 2: conversion = 12,150 / 4,50,000 = 2.7%, AOV = 70,47,000 / 12,150 = ₹580. Factors: sessions 0.90 (−10%), conversion 2.7 / 2.4 = 1.125 (+12.5%), AOV 580 / 600 = 0.967 (−3.3%). Revenue = 70,47,000 / 72,00,000 − 1 = −2.1%, and the biggest move is conversion: option A. Trap: option C adds the drivers (−10 + 12.5 − 3.3 ≈ −0.8%); option B picks sessions just because the drop feels bigger, but 12.5 > 10.

ba-w1-q13.question: A support team's KPI is '% of tickets resolved within SLA', with the RAG rule: ≥ 85% Green, 80–85% Amber, < 80% Red. This week: Agent P 170 / 200, Q 9 / 10, R 19 / 20, S 240 / 320. What is the team's correct SLA % and RAG status?
options: 86.25%, Green
80.0%, Amber
87.5%, Green
ba-w1-q13.explanation: Ratio of totals: (170 + 9 + 19 + 240) / (200 + 10 + 20 + 320) = 438 / 550 = 79.6%, which is below 80%, so Red (option B). Trap: option A is the simple average of the four agent rates (85, 90, 95, 75), which gives tiny Q and R the same weight as big S and wrongly shows Green; option D is the median of those rates, and option C is just the average of P and S.

ba-w1-q14.question: A store currently gets 2,00,000 sessions/month with 3% conversion. A paid campaign will bring 50,000 extra sessions that convert at only 1.5%. AOV stays the same. After the campaign, what are the overall conversion and the revenue growth?
options: Conversion stays at 3%, revenue +25%
Conversion 2.25%, revenue +12.5%
Conversion 2.7%, revenue +12.5%
Conversion 2.7%, revenue +25%
ba-w1-q14.explanation: Orders: 2,00,000 × 0.03 = 6,000 existing + 50,000 × 0.015 = 750 new = 6,750. Overall conversion = 6,750 / 2,50,000 = 2.7%. AOV is unchanged, so revenue growth = order growth = 6,750 / 6,000 − 1 = 12.5%, giving option C. Trap: option B takes the simple average of 3% and 1.5% (not a ratio of totals); options A and D treat the +25% session growth as revenue growth and ignore the fall in conversion.

ba-w1-q15.question: An app priced at ₹499/month has a 14-day free trial. Last month 1,500 trials started and 25% became paid. This month 1,200 trials started, and early data says 30% will become paid. How much new MRR will this month's trials bring, and how does it compare with the previous cohort?
options: ₹1,49,700; 20% less than the previous cohort
₹2,24,550; 20% more than the previous cohort
₹1,79,640; equal to the previous cohort
₹1,79,640; 4% less than the previous cohort
ba-w1-q15.explanation: This month: 1,200 × 0.30 × 499 = ₹1,79,640. Previous cohort: 1,500 × 0.25 × 499 = ₹1,87,125. Ratio = 1,79,640 / 1,87,125 = 0.96, i.e. 4% less: option D. Trap: option C assumes trials −20% and conversion +20% (25 → 30) cancel out, but factors multiply (0.8 × 1.2 = 0.96); option A applies the old 25% rate and option B uses the old 1,500 trials.

ba-w2-q7.question: In an orders table each row is one order (order_id, customer_id, amount). The manager asks: 'How many customers ordered this month?' Which aggregation is right in the pivot?
options: Simple count of order_id
Sum of the amount column
Distinct count of customer_id
Mean of the amount column
ba-w2-q7.explanation: One customer can place many orders, so counting customers needs the distinct count of customer_id: option C. Trap: option A counts orders, not customers, and double-counts repeat buyers; options B and D answer questions about revenue and order size.

ba-w2-q8.question: Of a gift shop's 10 orders, 9 were for ₹300 and one corporate order was for ₹20,300. The mean is ₹2,300 and the median is ₹300. What should be reported for 'how much a typical customer order is'?
options: Mean ₹2,300, because it counts every order
Median ₹300, because one big order is pulling the mean
Total ₹23,000, because that is the whole revenue
Largest order ₹20,300, because it is important
ba-w2-q8.explanation: The data are skewed: one ₹20,300 order drags the mean up to ₹2,300, while 9 of the 10 orders are ₹300. For a typical order the median ₹300 (option B) is right; ideally show both. Trap: option A sounds fair because it "includes every order", but here it looks like no real order at all; options C and D do not measure typical size.

ba-w2-q9.question: A grocery app wants to split customers into segments. Which of these is a **behavioural** segmentation?
options: By city tier: metro vs tier-2
By app language: Hindi vs English
By RFM score: recency, frequency, monetary
ba-w2-q9.explanation: RFM (option D) is based on what the customer actually buys: how recently, how often and how much. Trap: option C also seems tied to app usage, but language is a profile attribute, not behaviour; option A is geographic and option B is demographic segmentation.

ba-w2-q10.question: A bank has 2,000 mobile-banking users: in Metro 600 App + 400 Web, in Tier-2 300 App + 700 Web. The product head asks: 'What % of Web users are from Tier-2?'
ba-w2-q10.explanation: The question is about Web users, so the denominator is the Web column total: 400 + 700 = 1,100. Tier-2 Web = 700, so 700 / 1,100 = 63.6% (option A). Trap: option B is 700 / 1,000, i.e. "what % of Tier-2 users are on Web" (row %), which is a different question; option C is Metro's share of Web users and option D is Tier-2's share of App users.

ba-w2-q11.question: A chain ranks its stores by complaint rate (complaints / orders), with a rule that only stores with at least 100 orders enter the ranking. Data: Store A 3 / 12, B 30 / 150, C 45 / 300, D 8 / 40, E 26 / 200. Which store gets the 'worst' flag?
options: Store A (25%)
Store D (20%)
Store B (20%)
Store E (13%)
ba-w2-q11.explanation: First keep the stores with n ≥ 100: B (150), C (300), E (200). Their rates: B 30 / 150 = 20%, C 15%, E 13%. B is highest, so option C. Trap: option A's 25% looks biggest, but it rests on just 12 orders (a difference of 3 complaints swings the rate a lot); option B (Store D) has the same rate as B but its 40 orders are below the minimum.

ba-w2-q12.question: First-call resolution for two call centres (fictional): Centre X: simple tickets 450 / 500, complex 150 / 300. Centre Y: simple 190 / 200, complex 330 / 600. Standardising to the combined ticket mix (simple 700, complex 900), which centre is better and by how many percentage points?
options: X, by 10 percentage points (75% vs 65%)
Y, by 5 percentage points (72.5% vs 67.5%)
Y, by 10 percentage points (75% vs 65%)
They are equal, because both have 800 tickets
ba-w2-q12.explanation: Rates: X simple 90%, complex 50%; Y simple 95%, complex 55%. Common mix: simple 700 / 1,600 = 0.4375, complex 0.5625. X = 0.4375 × 90 + 0.5625 × 50 = 67.5%; Y = 0.4375 × 95 + 0.5625 × 55 = 72.5%. Y is ahead by 5 pp: option B. Trap: option A compares the crude overall rates (600 / 800 = 75% vs 520 / 800 = 65%) and falls into Simpson's paradox, since Y got 75% complex tickets; option C attaches the wrong label, and option D only looks at the total count.

ba-w2-q13.question: A website's visitors: last year New 1,000 (conversion 2%), Returning 1,000 (8%), overall 5%. This year New 3,000 (2.5%), Returning 1,000 (9%). If we keep the old 50-50 mix and apply the new rates, what would conversion be, and how big is the mix effect?
options: 5.75%; mix effect −1.625 pp
5.75%; mix effect +0.75 pp
4.125%; mix effect −0.875 pp
5.0%; mix effect 0 pp
ba-w2-q13.explanation: Old mix, new rates: 0.5 × 2.5 + 0.5 × 9 = 5.75%, so the rate effect = 5.75 − 5 = +0.75 pp. Actual this year: (3,000 × 0.025 + 1,000 × 0.09) / 4,000 = 165 / 4,000 = 4.125%. Mix effect = 4.125 − 5.75 = −1.625 pp: option A. Trap: option B reports the rate effect as the mix effect; option C is the actual overall rate and the total change (−0.875 pp), not the mix effect; option D assumes the rates did not change.

ba-w2-q14.question: A month's orders are shown below. The manager asks: 'How much did the average customer spend this month?' What is the correct pivot answer?
ba-w2-q14.explanation: First sum at customer level: C1 = 1,000, C2 = 300, C3 = 2,000. Then take the mean of these three: 3,300 / 3 = ₹1,100 (option C). Trap: option A is the mean of the 6 orders (average order value), not average customer spend; option B is the median of customer spends, and option D is total revenue.

ba-w2-q15.question: An e-tailer's orders fell from 50,000 to 40,000, and the return rate rose from 8% to 10%. The ops manager says: 'Returns went up 25%, expand the returns team.' What is the correct reading?
options: Returned orders rose 25%, going from 4,000 to 5,000
Returned orders fell 20%, because orders fell
The return rate rose by a full 25 percentage points
Returned orders stayed at 4,000; the rate rose 2 pp
ba-w2-q15.explanation: Returned orders: before 50,000 × 0.08 = 4,000, now 40,000 × 0.10 = 4,000, so the volume is the same. The rate rose 2 pp (relative 2 / 8 = 25%), but that came from the shrinking denominator: option D. So there is no case for a bigger returns team, though the higher rate is a quality signal. Trap: option A mistakes the 25% relative rate change for a volume change; option C mixes up pp and percent; option B ignores the rise in the rate.

ba-w3-q7.question: An analyst wants to test the association between city and preferred snack brand. For a chi-square test of independence, what should the table cells contain?
options: The percentage share of each brand within each city
The number of customers (counts) in each city–brand combination
The average rating score of each brand within each city
The average monthly spend of each city–brand combination
ba-w3-q7.explanation: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E is built on raw frequencies, so the cells must hold counts: option B. Trap: option A (percentages) shows the same pattern, but the χ² value then comes out wrong for the sample size N; options C and D are averages, not categorical counts.

ba-w3-q8.question: A company claims its 4 detergent brands have market shares of 40 : 30 : 20 : 10. An analyst runs a goodness-of-fit chi-square test on a sample. How many degrees of freedom are there?
ba-w3-q8.explanation: Goodness-of-fit has a single variable, so df = categories − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3 (option A). Trap: option C wrongly applies the (r − 1)(c − 1) formula of the independence test, and option B treats the number of categories as df; option D is what a 4 × 4 table would give (3 × 3).

ba-w3-q9.question: A paint company picked a **separate fixed sample of 200 customers** in each of Lucknow, Nagpur and Kochi and asked which finish (matte / gloss / satin) they prefer. Which chi-square test is this?
options: Goodness-of-fit test
Test of independence
Test of homogeneity
Two-sample t-test
ba-w3-q9.explanation: A separate fixed sample was taken from each city to ask whether the finish distribution is the same across the three populations, so this is a homogeneity test (option C); the arithmetic is the same as for independence. Trap: option B would apply if one random sample were classified by both city and finish; option A compares one variable with a claimed distribution, and option D is for numeric means.

ba-w3-q10.question: A survey table has N = 400. Which of these cells fails the 'E ≥ 5' rule for expected counts?
options: Row total 120, column total 150
Row total 80, column total 60
Row total 200, column total 25
Row total 40, column total 30
ba-w3-q10.explanation: E = row total × column total / N. Option A: 120 × 150 / 400 = 45; B: 80 × 60 / 400 = 12; C: 200 × 25 / 400 = 12.5; D: 40 × 30 / 400 = 3. Only option D has E < 5, so that category needs merging. Trap: option C has the smallest column total, 25, but its large row total makes E = 12.5, which is fine; the rule applies to the expected count, not to observed counts or margins.

ba-w3-q11.question: A telecom company claims its plan shares are Basic 50%, Plus 30%, Max 20%. A sample of 200 customers had 90 Basic, 70 Plus, 40 Max. What is the result of a goodness-of-fit test at the 5% level (critical value 5.991 at df = 2)?
options: χ² ≈ 2.67, reject H₀: the claim is wrong
χ² ≈ 2.67, do not reject H₀: the data are consistent with the claim
χ² ≈ 26.7, reject H₀: the claim is wrong
χ² ≈ 1.67, do not reject H₀: the data are consistent with the claim
ba-w3-q11.explanation: Expected: 200 × 0.5 = 100, 200 × 0.3 = 60, 200 × 0.2 = 40. χ² = (90 − 100)² / 100 + (70 − 60)² / 60 + (40 − 40)² / 40 = 1 + 1.667 + 0 = 2.67. Since 2.67 < 5.991, H₀ is not rejected: option B. Trap: option A takes the opposite decision on the same number; option C is a decimal shift, and option D is only the Plus contribution and forgets Basic.

ba-w3-q12.question: A juice brand survey (fictional): Delhi (200): Mango 80, Guava 70, Litchi 50. Mumbai (200): Mango 60, Guava 70, Litchi 70. What is the result of an independence test at the 5% level (critical 5.991 at df = 2), and what is Cramér's V?
options: χ² ≈ 6.19, reject H₀; V ≈ 0.12
χ² ≈ 6.19, do not reject H₀ because 6.19 < 9.488
χ² ≈ 3.10, do not reject H₀; V ≈ 0.09
χ² ≈ 6.19, reject H₀; V ≈ 0.02
ba-w3-q12.explanation: Column totals are 140, 140, 120 and N = 400, so E = 70, 70, 60 in both rows. Contributions in each row: (10)² / 70 = 1.43, 0, (10)² / 60 = 1.67; over both rows χ² = 2 × 3.10 = 6.19 > 5.991, so reject H₀. k = min(2, 3) = 2, V = √(6.19 / (400 × 1)) ≈ 0.12: option A. Trap: option B uses the df = 4 critical value though the table is 2 × 3; option C sums only one row, and option D forgets the square root (6.19 / 400 ≈ 0.015).

ba-w3-q13.question: Below are the observed (O) and expected (E) counts for four cells of a significant chi-square test. Which statement is the most accurate to give the manager?
options: Bhopal–N drives the result most, because O − E = 20 is the largest
In Jaipur, Brand K sells far less than expected (residual ≈ −2.47)
In Jaipur, Brand K over-indexes (residual ≈ +2.47)
Indore–M has the largest residual, ≈ 1.83, so it drives the result
ba-w3-q13.explanation: Standardised residual = (O − E) / √E. Jaipur–K: −14 / √32 ≈ −2.47; Surat–L: 11 / 8 = 1.38; Indore–M: 10 / √30 ≈ 1.83; Bhopal–N: 20 / 10 = 2.0. The largest |residual| is Jaipur–K and its sign is negative, so Brand K is less preferred there than expected: option B. Trap: option A looks at raw O − E, which favours cells with a large E; option C reads the sign the wrong way, and option D misses both Jaipur and Bhopal.

ba-w3-q14.question: A 3 × 3 table (income band × brand) has N = 500 and Cramér's V = 0.10. The 5% critical value at df = 4 is 9.488. Which statement is correct?
options: χ² = 5, H₀ is not rejected
χ² = 50, the association is strong
χ² = 10, H₀ is rejected, but the association is weak
χ² = 10, H₀ is not rejected because V < 0.3
ba-w3-q14.explanation: From V = √(χ² / (N(k − 1))), χ² = V² × N × (k − 1) = 0.01 × 500 × 2 = 10. Since 10 > 9.488, H₀ is rejected; but V = 0.10 is a weak association: option C. Trap: option A forgets the (k − 1) factor; option B uses V instead of V² (0.10 × 500), and option D treats the effect size as the significance test, though they answer different questions.

ba-w3-q15.question: A retailer's 300 transactions: Online 150 (UPI 105, Card 45), Store 150 (UPI 75, Card 75). What is the result of testing independence of channel and payment mode (5% critical 3.841 at df = 1, no continuity correction)?
options: χ² ≈ 3.54; H₀ is not rejected
χ² = 6.25; reject H₀; φ ≈ 0.14
χ² = 12.5; reject H₀; φ ≈ 0.04
χ² = 12.5; reject H₀; φ ≈ 0.20
ba-w3-q15.explanation: Column totals are UPI 180, Card 120, N = 300, so in each row E = 90 (UPI) and 60 (Card). Every cell has |O − E| = 15: χ² = 225 / 90 + 225 / 60 + 225 / 90 + 225 / 60 = 2.5 + 3.75 + 2.5 + 3.75 = 12.5 > 3.841, so reject. φ = √(12.5 / 300) ≈ 0.20: option D. Trap: option A takes the square root of χ²; option B adds the contributions of only one row, and option C forgets the root in φ (12.5 / 300 ≈ 0.04).

ba-w4-q7.question: An insurance website tests two landing pages. For each visitor the outcome is just 'took a quote / did not', and the two pages get different visitors. Which test is right?
options: Two-proportion z-test
Welch two-sample t-test
One-way ANOVA
Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
ba-w4-q7.explanation: The outcome is binary and there are two independent groups, so the two-proportion z-test (option A), which compares two proportions, is right. Trap: option B is for means of a numeric outcome (like average premium); option C is for means of three or more groups, and option D compares a single variable with a claimed distribution.

ba-w4-q8.question: An ANOVA is to be run on the average basket value of three store formats. Group SDs: ₹4, ₹5 and ₹11 (in hundreds). By the rule of thumb, what should be done?
options: Ordinary one-way ANOVA, because there are 3 groups
Three pairwise pooled t-tests
Ordinary ANOVA, because all three SDs are below 15
Welch ANOVA, because the SD ratio 11 / 4 = 2.75 > 2
ba-w4-q8.explanation: Equal-variance check: largest SD / smallest SD = 11 / 4 = 2.75, which is above 2, so equal variances cannot be assumed and Welch ANOVA (option D) is needed. Trap: options A and C ignore the equal-variance assumption (the rule is about the ratio, not any absolute SD); option B inflates the error rate with multiple t-tests, and its pooled variance makes the same wrong assumption.

ba-w4-q9.question: A new onboarding flow raised average session time by 6 minutes. The pooled SD of both groups is 12 minutes. What is Cohen's d?
ba-w4-q9.explanation: Cohen's d = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / pooled SD = 6 / 12 = 0.5 (option C), usually seen as a medium-sized effect. Trap: option A flips the ratio (12 / 6); option B is just the raw difference, not standardised; option D has a misplaced decimal.

ba-w4-q10.question: Two sales training programmes: A has 36 reps, average monthly sales ₹520 (thousand), s = 60; B has 25 reps, average ₹490, s = 50. What is the result of a Welch t-test (two-sided, α = 0.05; t critical 2.003 at df ≈ 56)?
options: t ≈ 2.12, reject H₀
t = 1.50, do not reject H₀
t ≈ 15.7, reject H₀
t ≈ 2.12, do not reject H₀
ba-w4-q10.explanation: v_A = 60² / 36 = 100, v_B = 50² / 25 = 100. SE = √(100 + 100) ≈ 14.14, t = (520 − 490) / 14.14 ≈ 2.12 > 2.003, so reject H₀: option A. Trap: option B adds the SEs (10 + 10 = 20) when it is the variances that add; option C divides s by n without squaring it; option D takes the wrong decision on the correct t.

ba-w4-q11.question: An ANOVA across 3 discount levels gave SSB = 48 and SSW = 152. What is η², and what does it mean?
options: 0.24; 24% of the variation in sales is explained by discount level
0.316; 31.6% of the variation in sales is explained by discount level
0.76; 76% of the variation in sales is explained by discount level
4.26; the discount effect is 4.26 times as large
ba-w4-q11.explanation: SST = SSB + SSW = 48 + 152 = 200, η² = SSB / SST = 48 / 200 = 0.24: option A. Trap: option B uses SSB / SSW (wrong denominator); option C is the within-group share (152 / 200), the unexplained part; option D looks like an F-statistic, not an effect size.

ba-w4-q12.question: A checkout A/B test: A had 200 orders from 4,000 visitors, B had 248 orders from 4,000 visitors. What are the result of a pooled two-proportion z-test (two-sided, α = 0.05, critical 1.96) and the lift?
options: z ≈ 2.33; significant; lift of 24 percentage points
z ≈ 2.33; significant; lift of 1.2 pp, i.e. 24% relative
z ≈ 1.65; not significant; lift of 1.2 pp
z ≈ 2.33; not significant, because the lift is only 1.2 pp
ba-w4-q12.explanation: p̂_A = 5%, p̂_B = 6.2%. Pooled p̂ = 448 / 8,000 = 0.056, SE = √(0.056 × 0.944 × (1/4,000 + 1/4,000)) ≈ 0.00514, z = 0.012 / 0.00514 ≈ 2.33 > 1.96, so significant. Lift = 1.2 pp, relative 1.2 / 5 = 24%: option B. Trap: option A calls the relative lift percentage points; option D treats a small absolute lift as evidence against significance (significance is decided by z); option C has the wrong z.

ba-w4-q13.question: 3 packaging designs, each in 5 stores (N = 15). The group means of weekly units are 20, 24, 28, and each group has SD 4. What are the F, the decision and η² of a one-way ANOVA (5% critical for F(2, 12) is 3.885)?
options: F = 1.0, do not reject H₀
F = 5.0, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.83
F = 5.0, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.45
F ≈ 5.83, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.45
ba-w4-q13.explanation: Grand mean 24. SSB = 5 × ((20 − 24)² + 0 + (28 − 24)²) = 5 × 32 = 160, MSB = 160 / 2 = 80. SSW = 3 × (5 − 1) × 4² = 192, MSW = 192 / 12 = 16. F = 80 / 16 = 5.0 > 3.885, reject. η² = 160 / (160 + 192) ≈ 0.45: option C. Trap: option A forgets to multiply SSB by the group size 5 (SSB = 32); option B uses η² = SSB / SSW; option D divides MSW by N − 1 = 14 instead of N − k = 12.

ba-w4-q14.question: An ANOVA across 4 delivery partners was significant. The p-values of all pairwise tests are: 0.004, 0.012, 0.030, 0.0009, 0.20, 0.06. After a Bonferroni correction at family-wise α = 0.05, how many pairs differ significantly?
options: 4 pairs
3 pairs
1 pair
2 pairs
ba-w4-q14.explanation: 4 groups ⇒ m = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6 pairs, each tested at 0.05 / 6 ≈ 0.0083. Only 0.004 and 0.0009 are smaller, so 2 pairs: option D. Trap: option A compares with 0.05 without correction; option B divides by m = 4 (the number of groups), giving 0.0125, which lets 0.012 through too; option C counts only the smallest p-value.

ba-w4-q15.question: Picking time for two warehouse layouts: Layout A: n = 40, mean 50 sec, s = 5. Layout B: n = 10, mean 44 sec, s = 15. The pooled t comes out ≈ 2.15 (critical 2.011 at df = 48). Using the Welch test (df ≈ 9.5; critical 2.262 at df = 9), what is the correct report?
options: Report pooled t ≈ 2.15: significant, because total n = 50
Welch t ≈ 1.25, not significant; SDs of 5 vs 15 are very different
Welch t ≈ 2.15, significant, because both tests give the same t
Welch t ≈ 1.25, significant, because 1.25 > 1
ba-w4-q15.explanation: Welch: v_A = 5² / 40 = 0.625, v_B = 15² / 10 = 22.5, SE = √23.125 ≈ 4.81, t = 6 / 4.81 ≈ 1.25 < 2.262, so not significant: option B. The pooled t is wrong here because the SD ratio 15 / 5 = 3 > 2 and the sizes are very unequal; the pooled variance understates the small, noisy group B. Trap: option A trusts the pooled test because of the larger total n; option C assumes both tests give the same t; option D compares t with 1 instead of the critical value.

ba-w5-q7.question: An intern regresses 10 years of daily **share prices** of two companies on each other and gets R² = 0.92. A senior analyst says the result cannot be trusted. What is the best reason?
options: R² is always close to 1 for prices, so 0.92 is low
Both series trend; a high R² appears even with no real relation
10 years of daily data is far too little for a regression
Regression only works on positive numbers, not on prices
ba-w5-q7.explanation: Regressing trending price series gives a high R² from the shared trend even when there is no real relation (spurious regression); that is why analysis is done on returns: option B. Trap: option C sounds reasonable, but 10 years of daily data is plenty; options A and D are false statements about regression.

ba-w5-q8.question: An FMCG stock's market model is R̂ᵢ = 0 + 0.7·R_m (both in %). If the market falls 4% in a month, what is the stock's expected return?
ba-w5-q8.explanation: R̂ᵢ = 0.7 × (−4) = −2.8% (option A). With β = 0.7 < 1 the stock is defensive and falls less than the market. Trap: option C divides 4 by 0.7; option B adds 4 and 0.7, and option D drops the sign.

ba-w5-q9.question: A pharma stock's market model has R² = 0.35. What does this correctly mean?
options: The correlation of stock and market returns is 0.35
The stock's β is 0.35, so it is a defensive stock
35% of variance is from the market, 65% company-specific
The stock returns 35% more than the market each month
ba-w5-q9.explanation: R² = the market-explained (systematic) share of the stock's return variance = 35%; the remaining 1 − 0.35 = 65% is idiosyncratic and can be reduced by diversification: option C. Trap: option A treats R² as r (here r = √0.35 ≈ 0.59); option B mixes up R² and β, which are different things; option D is about the return level, not the variance.

ba-w5-q10.question: A market model on 60 monthly returns gave b = 1.4 and SE(b) = 0.16 (two-sided 5% t critical ≈ 2.002 at df = 58). Is the stock's β significantly different from 1?
options: t = 8.75; yes, β = 1 is clearly rejected
t = 2.5; no, because the gap between 1.4 and 1 is small
t = 0.4; no, β = 1 is not rejected at all
t = 2.5; yes, β = 1 is rejected, the stock is aggressive
ba-w5-q10.explanation: H₀: β = 1, so t = (b − 1) / SE = (1.4 − 1) / 0.16 = 2.5 > 2.002: reject, and since b > 1 the stock is aggressive: option D. Trap: option A is the default-output t = 1.4 / 0.16 = 8.75, which tests H₀: β = 0; option C forgets to divide by SE (1.4 − 1 = 0.4); option B takes the wrong decision on the right t.

ba-w5-q11.question: A sales model with 4 predictors was fitted on 25 quarters of data and gave R² = 0.50. What is the overall F-statistic (H₀: all slopes are 0)?
ba-w5-q11.explanation: F = (R² / k) / ((1 − R²) / (n − k − 1)) = (0.50 / 4) / (0.50 / 20) = 0.125 / 0.025 = 5.0 (option A). Trap: option B is just R² / (1 − R²) and forgets the degrees of freedom; option C uses n − 1 = 24 in the denominator; option D divides the numerator by k + 1 = 5.

ba-w5-q12.question: 5 monthly returns (%) for Kaveri Textiles (fictional) and the market: R_m = 2, 0, −1, 3, 1; Rᵢ = 2.5, 0.5, −1.5, 1.5, −0.5. What are the market model's β, α and R²?
ba-w5-q12.explanation: Means: R̄_m = 1, R̄ᵢ = 0.5. Market deviations 1, −1, −2, 2, 0 ⇒ Sxx = 10; stock deviations 2, 0, −2, 1, −1 ⇒ Sxy = 2 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 8, Syy = 10. β = 8 / 10 = 0.8, α = 0.5 − 0.8 × 1 = −0.3, R² = 8² / (10 × 10) = 0.64: option C. Trap: option D reports r = 0.8 as R²; option B takes α as just the stock mean; option A flips β to Sxx / Sxy.

ba-w5-q13.question: An analyst regressed weekly sales on ad spend alone and got a slope of 1.8. The true model also has store footfall, with coefficient 0.6, and regressing footfall on ad spend gives a slope of 0.5. What is the true partial effect of ad spend (footfall held constant)?
ba-w5-q13.explanation: OVB: simple slope = β₁ + β₂ · δ, so 1.8 = β₁ + 0.6 × 0.5 = β₁ + 0.3, giving β₁ = 1.5 (option D). The simple slope was biased upward because footfall raises sales (β₂ > 0) and rises with ad spend (δ > 0). Trap: option A adds the bias instead of removing it; option B takes the simple slope as the partial effect; option C computes 1.8 × 0.5, which has no meaning here.

ba-w5-q14.question: Two models on 31 months of data: Model 1 (2 predictors) R² = 0.60; Model 2 (6 predictors) R² = 0.63. By adjusted R², which model is better?
options: Model 1: adjusted R² ≈ 0.571 vs 0.538
Model 2: R² 0.63 > 0.60, so it is better
Model 2: 4 extra predictors raised R² by 3 points
They are equal: both have adjusted R² ≈ 0.55
ba-w5-q14.explanation: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1) / (n − k − 1). Model 1: 1 − 0.40 × 30 / 28 ≈ 0.571. Model 2: 1 − 0.37 × 30 / 24 ≈ 0.538. Model 1 is ahead: option A. Trap: options B and C look at plain R², which never falls when a variable is added, even a useless one; option D is wrong arithmetic.

ba-w5-q15.question: A cement stock's monthly returns have SD 8%, the market's SD is 4%, and their correlation is r = 0.6. What are the market model's β, R², and the share of diversifiable (idiosyncratic) variance?
options: β = 0.3, R² = 0.36; 64% of variance diversifiable
β = 1.2, R² = 0.36; 64% of variance diversifiable
β = 1.2, R² = 0.6; 40% of variance diversifiable
β = 2.0, R² = 0.36; 36% of variance diversifiable
ba-w5-q15.explanation: β = Cov / Var(R_m) = r × σᵢ / σ_m = 0.6 × 8 / 4 = 1.2. R² = r² = 0.36, so the idiosyncratic share = 1 − 0.36 = 64%: option B. Trap: option A flips the SD ratio (0.6 × 4 / 8); option C takes r itself as R²; option D ignores the correlation, uses just σᵢ / σ_m, and calls the systematic share diversifiable.
